not to have to, not to need to

Use “lassen” + infinitive in the sense of “to allow”: Ich lasse dich schlafen.
Use “lassen” + infinitive in the sense of “to have someone else do something”: Ich lasse das Auto reparieren.

It's 24 December, ten o'clock in the morning. This year, Christmas is at Ludwig's, with the whole family, like in the old days. Mara comes to help. Ludwig wants to do everything himself.
Ludwig, what are you doing up that ladder? Come down at once! Let me do that!
I'm just hanging the star on the tree. I've been doing it for fifty years. Leave me in peace!
At eighty and with your back? No. I'm not letting you stand on the ladder. Give me the star.
All right, then. But you don't need to scold me like that. You sound like Ingrid.
I'll take that as a compliment. What else do we have to do?

The goose has to go in the oven. I cooked the red cabbage yesterday. And I still have to go to the hairdresser's. I'm having my hair cut today at twelve. Thomas mustn't think his father looks like an old rocker.
But you were a rocker back then! And the guitar? Have you had it tuned?
No. Today I'm letting Paul do that. He has a better ear than me. And he only needs a quarter of an hour.
And the food for this evening? Shall I cook something?
You don't need to cook anything at all. Lena's bringing the stollen, Kasia's bringing pierogi, and Thomas is bringing Bavarian sausages. You just need to come. And bring sarmale. Lots of sarmale.
Ha! So I do have to cook after all.
Sarmale aren't cooking. Sarmale are love. You said so yourself. And now let's finish decorating the tree.
peace, quiet (“in Ruhe lassen” = to leave in peace)
“brauchst nicht zu” = you don't need to
“lassen” → “du lässt, er lässt” = “lest”: a becomes ä.
“be-SHAY-roong”: the moment the presents are given out.
“fri-ZØR”: a French word, stress at the end.
“lassen” + infinitive (at the end, without “zu”) = to let someone do something:
Ludwig lets Paul tune the guitar.
I'm not letting you stand on the ladder.
2. Lassen: to have someone else do something
The second important meaning: you DON'T do it yourself, someone else does it for you (usually a professional):
I'm having my car repaired. (the mechanic repairs it)
I'm having my hair cut. (the hairdresser cuts it)

Watch the difference: “Ich schneide mir die Haare” = I cut my hair myself. “Ich lasse mir die Haare schneiden” = I go to the hairdresser's. (English works the same way: “I cut my hair” vs “I have my hair cut”.)
Perfekt: “Ich habe mir die Haare schneiden lassen” (double infinitive, not “gelassen”!). When “lassen” goes with another verb, its participle looks like the infinitive.
Ich habe den Schlüssel liegen lassen.
“nicht brauchen zu” = don't have to / don't need to. It means the same as “nicht müssen”:
You don't need to be afraid.
With “nur” or “bloß”, it means “only have to / just need to”:
You just need to sign here.
Unlike “müssen”, “brauchen” needs “zu”: “Du musst nicht kommen”, but “Du brauchst nicht zu kommen”.
“Ich lasse mir die Haare schneiden” means:
I have my hair cut at the hairdresser's.
I'm letting my hair grow long.

You don't need to be afraid.

At four in the afternoon the doorbell rang for the first time. Thomas was standing outside the door with his wife Katrin, the three children and so many bags you'd think they were staying for a month. Paul was carrying his guitar on his back and a bag of Bavarian sausages in his hand. Fritz smelt the sausages immediately and forgot all his good manners.

Ludwig opened the door. He had had his hair cut short and neat and was wearing a white shirt that Mara had ironed for him that morning, because she didn't want to leave him alone with the iron. Thomas looked at his father and laughed. “Dad, you look like you do in the wedding photo. Just without the long hair.”

Then the others came. Sabine from Potsdam, Lena's mother, who hugged Ludwig tightly and gave him a scarf she had knitted herself. Lena and Andrei, with the biggest stollen Kastanienallee had ever seen. The Nowak family with Kuba, Ola, Bruno and a huge bowl of pierogi. And last of all Mara, with a pot of sarmale so heavy that Andrei had to carry it up the stairs.

Only Mrs Hoffmann was still missing. Since the concert in March she hadn't been feeling so well. Her legs had grown weaker, and the stairs from the fourth floor were now impossible for her. But she absolutely wanted to be there. “Last year I walked down the stairs,” she had said. “This year I'll have myself carried. Like a queen.” So Thomas and Andrei carried her down the three floors on an old wooden chair, slowly, carefully, step by step, while Kuba walked ahead and shouted “Careful, bend!”. Mrs Hoffmann sat on the chair as straight as a candle, in her navy-blue dress, and waved to the neighbours as if she were riding through the streets of Vienna. When she reached the bottom, everyone applauded. “You don't need to applaud,” she said sternly. But she was smiling.

But the most important thing came at six. Jonas and Clara, for the first time with little Ludwig, ten days old, in a red romper suit with a yellow tram on it, which Lena had sewn. The boy was asleep. He slept when Ludwig took him in his arms. He slept when Kuba and Ola looked at him, wide-eyed and very quietly. He even slept when Fritz and Bruno barked at the same time, because someone had set off a rocket in the courtyard.
Let him sleep, Ludwig. He doesn't need to be awake. He was awake enough last night.

There was no room left in the flat. Thomas and Andrei had carried the table down from Mara's flat and put it next to Ludwig's table, and even so the children had to eat on the sofa. There were fourteen plates, twenty people, two dogs, a baby and a yellow lamp shining above them all. “Fourteen plates,” Ludwig said quietly to Mara. “Do you know how many plates we used to have? Ingrid and I? Two. And at Christmas four, with the children.”

After the meal, which lasted two hours and at which nobody stuck to a diet, it was time for presents. Kuba got a new collar for Bruno, Ola a book about horses. Lena got a ring from Andrei. Not an engagement ring, as he quickly explained when everyone shrieked, but a small silver ring with a bee on it, which his father had ordered from a jeweller in Sibiu. “For the queen,” said Andrei. Lena said nothing. But she wore it all evening and looked at it roughly every five minutes.

Ludwig got lots of presents, but one was different from the others. Paul gave him a flat parcel. Inside was a vinyl record, brand new, in a handmade sleeve. On it, it said: “The Rails. Live on Kastanienallee. 2028.” In the summer, at the eightieth birthday party, Paul had secretly recorded on his phone how he and Ludwig played together in the courtyard, and had had the recording pressed onto a real record, in a studio in Munich.
Grandpa, you always said “The Rails” never made a record, because it wasn't allowed in the GDR. Now you have one. The first one. Fifty years too late, but you can't complain.

Ludwig held the record in his hands for a long time. Then he stood up, went to the old record player that Mrs Hoffmann had lent him for the evening, and put it on. It crackled. Then two guitars could be heard in the living room, one old and one young, and in the background fairy lights humming softly, children's laughter and, right at the end, a piano from the fourth floor.

Nobody spoke. Thomas put his arm around his father's shoulders. Sabine was crying quietly. Little Ludwig woke up, looked around with his big dark eyes and fell asleep again, as if he had decided that everything was all right.

At midnight, when the guests had left and only Mara was still helping with the washing-up, Ludwig sat down on his sofa under the yellow lamp. He looked at the fourteen plates in the sink, at the record on the record player, at Fritz, who was snoring full and happy on the rug. “Mara,” he said, “leave that. Leave the plates. They can wait until tomorrow. Sit with me.” Mara sat down. They sat like that for a long time, without speaking, and listened as it began to snow outside.

Shortly before Mara left, there was another soft knock at the door. It was Andrei. He had carried Mrs Hoffmann back up to the fourth floor, together with Thomas, and then stayed with her for another half an hour, because she wanted to tell him about her first Christmas after the war. “She said this was the most beautiful Christmas in fifty years,” he said. “And that I had to pass something on to you.” Mara asked what. Andrei smiled. “She said: take your time, child. But don't take too much time. Life doesn't wait.” Mara didn't really understand what she meant. But she knew that one day she would.
Outside, the snow was falling on the chestnut tree, on the roofs, on the tram rails, softly and white, like in an old carol.

Read the text about German Christmas customs. Listen twice. At the end there are 4 questions.
In Germany, the Christmas season begins with Advent, four Sundays before Christmas. Every Sunday a candle is lit on the Advent wreath.
The most important day isn't the 25th but 24 December, Christmas Eve. In the evening the presents are given out.
Many families don't decorate the tree until the 24th, often the parents do it while the children have to wait.
The traditional dishes are goose with red cabbage and dumplings, or simply frankfurters with potato salad.
And German stollen, a heavy bread with raisins and icing sugar, you don't have to bake yourself. You can buy it. But home-baked tastes better.
